exemplar_points.a: Hacker offers an economic interpretation: the Revolution was a struggle to preserve English mercantile capitalism against colonial competition, not a battle of constitutional ideas. Bailyn offers an ideological interpretation: colonists genuinely feared a deliberate conspiracy against liberty, and that fear — not economics — drove the Revolution.
exemplar_points.b: Parliament's post-1763 revenue program — the Sugar Act (1764) and Stamp Act (1765), designed to make colonists pay for imperial defense and administration — supports Hacker's economic reading: the flashpoints were taxes and trade regulation protecting English commercial interests.
exemplar_points.c: The colonial reaction to the Coercive Acts (1774) — widely read as proof that Parliament intended to enslave America, prompting the Continental Congress and extralegal committees — supports Bailyn: colonists acted on a sincere belief in an orchestrated conspiracy against their liberties.

parts.c: Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development during the period 1754 to 1783 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Bailyn's interpretation.

questions.stimulus: Excerpt 1: Historian Andrew Hacker argues the Revolution cannot be understood apart from English imperial economic policy, which had aimed since Cromwell's era at protecting English capitalist interests. When colonial economic competition jeopardized those interests, London insisted only where fundamental mercantile principles were at stake. The struggle, in this view, was not truly about taxation powers or natural rights but about the survival of English mercantile capitalism within the imperial system. (Paraphrased from Andrew Hacker, The Triumph of American Capitalism, 1940.) Excerpt 2: Historian Bernard Bailyn argues that the language of 'slavery,' 'corruption,' and 'conspiracy' in Revolutionary writing was not mere propaganda. Used forcefully across social classes, positions, and denominations, these words reflected genuine fear and anxiety: colonists sincerely believed a comprehensive conspiracy against liberty — nourished by corruption, with American oppression its most visible part — lay at the heart of British policy. (Paraphrased from Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, 1967.)

questions.stimulus: "The government itself, which is only the mode which the people have chosen to execute their will, is equally liable to be abused and perverted before the people can act through it. Witness the present Mexican war, the work of comparatively a few individuals using the standing government as their tool; for, in the outset, the people would not have consented to this measure. . . . Law never made men a whit more just; and, by means of their respect for it, even the well-disposed are daily made the agents of injustice. A common and natural result of an undue respect for law is, that you may see a file of soldiers, colonel, captain, corporal, privates, power-monkeys, and all, marching in admirable order over hill and dale to wars, against their wills, ay, against their common sense and consciences, which makes it very steep marching indeed, and produces a palpitation of the heart. . . . There are thousands who are in opinion opposed to slavery and to the war, who yet in effect do nothing to put an end to them; who, esteeming themselves children of Washington and Franklin, sit down with their hands in their pockets, and say that they know not what to do, and do nothing." — Henry David Thoreau, On the Duty of Civil Disobedience, 1846

parts.a: Briefly describe Thoreau's perspective in regard to the people who are 'in opinion opposed' to the Mexican War.
parts.b: Briefly describe ONE specific historical development in the period 1820 to 1846 that contributed to the 'present Mexican war' mentioned in the excerpt.
parts.c: Briefly describe one effect of the Mexican War in the period 1848 to 1865.

questions.scoring_notes: (a) 1 pt: describes Thoreau's contempt — the merely 'in opinion opposed' are moral cowards who deplore the war and slavery yet do nothing, waiting passively for others to act while their respect for law makes them agents of injustice. (b) 1 pt: describes a causal 1820–1846 development — e.g., the Texas Revolution (1836) and annexation of Texas (1845); the ideology of Manifest Destiny; Polk's expansionist election in 1844 and his provocation on the Rio Grande. (c) 1 pt: describes an 1848–1865 effect — e.g., the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo's vast territorial cession; the Wilmot Proviso debate inflaming sectional conflict over slavery's extension; the Compromise of 1850 as an attempt to settle that conflict. Each part scored independently.

exemplar_points.a: Thoreau views the passively opposed with scorn: they pride themselves as 'children of Washington and Franklin' yet sit 'with their hands in their pockets,' regretting and petitioning but doing 'nothing in earnest' — their deference to law makes even the well-disposed complicit in injustice.
exemplar_points.b: The annexation of Texas in 1845 — following the Texas Revolution of 1836 — directly produced the war: Polk's insistence on the Rio Grande boundary and his dispatch of troops into disputed territory provoked the clash he used to ask Congress for a war declaration.
exemplar_points.c: The war's territorial spoils detonated the slavery-extension crisis: David Wilmot's 1846 proviso demanding slavery's exclusion from Mexican cession lands split Congress along sectional lines, beginning the decade-long unraveling that led to the Compromise of 1850 and, eventually, secession.

A thin, poorly dressed rider wearing a cap marked 'Labor' sits astride a bony, tired horse; facing him is an armored knight marked 'Monopoly' whose mount is a mighty steam locomotive. The contest is visibly rigged: corporate power, armored and engine-driven, overwhelms the defenseless worker.

parts.a: Briefly describe ONE perspective about economics and politics in the 1880s expressed in the image.
parts.b: Briefly explain ONE specific event or development that led to the perspective expressed in the image.
parts.c: Briefly explain ONE specific effect of the historical development referenced by the image.

questions.scoring_notes: (a) 1 pt: describes the cartoon's pro-labor perspective — e.g., sympathy for workers facing impossible odds; the 'tournament' of Gilded Age capitalism is rigged, with armored, locomotive-powered monopoly capital crushing defenseless labor; the deck is stacked for corporate owners. (b) 1 pt: explains a causal development — e.g., the rise of trusts and monopolies (Standard Oil, U.S. Steel, railroad combinations) concentrating power over workers; crushing defeats of labor in strikes such as the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, with corporations deploying strikebreakers and state/federal force. (c) 1 pt: explains an effect — e.g., workers turning to unions and collective action (Knights of Labor, AFL); public and political backlash producing antitrust sentiment and eventually the Sherman Anti-Trust Act (1890) and Interstate Commerce Act (1887). Each part scored independently.

exemplar_points.a: The cartoon expresses the era's labor-sympathetic view that Gilded Age capitalism was a fixed fight: 'Monopoly,' clad in armor and riding steam power, cannot lose against 'Labor,' a starved figure on a broken-down horse — corporate owners held all the weapons in workplace conflicts.
exemplar_points.b: The perspective grew from the consolidation of trusts and monopolies that dominated industries like oil refining and railroads, combined with labor's shattering defeats — as in the Great Railroad Strike of 1877 — when corporations used replacement workers and government troops to break strikes.
exemplar_points.c: The imbalance the cartoon depicts drove workers into mass organization: the Knights of Labor swelled to hundreds of thousands of members in the 1880s, and the demand to curb concentrated corporate power fed the antitrust movement culminating in the Sherman Act of 1890.
